claims.text: Advanced alloying techniques can enhance both strength and ductility in metallic materials.
Conventional metallic alloys exhibit a strength–ductility trade-off.
Adding specific elements is an advanced alloying technique capable of addressing the trade-off.
Novel processing methods can be used to address the strength–ductility trade-off.
The induced microstructure can provide solid-solution strengthening.
The induced microstructure can provide precipitation hardening.
Alloying-induced microstructural modification improves dislocation movement.
Alloying-induced microstructural modification improves grain-boundary interactions.
Improved dislocation movement and grain-boundary interactions enhance both strength and ductility.
Advanced alloying will increase tensile strength relative to conventional processing.
Advanced alloying will increase ductility relative to conventional processing.
The proposed hypothesis is scoped to metallic alloys and may not generalize to nonmetallic materials.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the alloying elements and processing techniques used.

contradictions.description: Solid-solution strengthening and precipitation hardening are named as strengthening mediators, but the mechanism attributes strengthening to vaguely 'improved dislocation movement.' The hypothesis does not reconcile this with the usual role of these strengthening modes in impeding or controlling dislocation motion.
